Boil, boil, toil and trouble… what bewitching book will you find at the Education Library?

event.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
event.description:
Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material.

Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions. Institutional Seat (2022) modifies a standard bench from the museum’s galleries into a version that is more comfortable for all museum visitors. Surround Sound (2022) attends to the floor of the gallery with dance-floor materials. Over the course of the exhibition, this floor will collect marks made by visitors’ shoes, strollers, and wheelchair treads, like another form of tally or notation.

Carolyn Lazard (b. 1987) is a New York-based artist whose primary medium is iteration. They also work across video, sculpture, installation, and performance. Their practice remembers the generative incapacity of debility.

Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is organized by the Cantor Arts Center, presenting work originally co-commissioned by the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis; the Institute of Contemporary Art, University of Pennsylvania; and Nottingham Contemporary, and is curated by Christina Linden, Director of Academic and Public Programs. We gratefully acknowledge support from The Lynn Krywick Gibbons Gallery Exhibitions Fund at the Cantor Arts Center.

event.title: JANE! An intimate exploration of Gilded Age excess  and the enigmatic life and death of Jane Stanford
event.description:
Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

From her elegant French gowns to a colossal painting of her jewels, from the Egyptian artifacts she acquired for her fledgling museum to a Hawaiian skirt she may or may not have purchased immediately before her suspicious death, Jane! presents various idiosyncratic artifacts of Stanford lore—many shown for the very first time, and very likely for the last.

IMAGE: Napoleon T. Sarony, Portrait of Jane Lathrop Stanford, 1871. Photograph with charcoal touch up, 55 ½ x 45 in. Cantor Arts Center, Stanford University, Stanford Family Collections, JLS.18217

event.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
event.description:
The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future. The exhibition explores Kim’s concept of “Indigenous Futures” through art as a form of civilizational transformation, expressing p'owŏl (포월 抱越), embracing and transcending the pain and contradictions of reality while reaching toward new possibilities for the future.

The opening reception on October 8 will feature an artist talk and a Korean mask dance (탈춤 t'alch'um) performance by Kim Bong-Jun and Che Se-hyun, a Seattle-based creative director and multidisciplinary artist.

The exhibition is curated by Jee-Young Park, Korean Studies Librarian, and Jisoo Kim, an SFSU MA Museum Studies graduate and San Francisco-based curator.

event.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
event.description:
Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France. Though commercially unsuccessful, these experiments laid the groundwork for the scanning, machining, and printing technologies ubiquitous today. Bringing together these rare artifacts, the exhibition opens up a little-known chapter of history to reveal the roots and richness of our contemporary world. An accompanying catalogue features four newly commissioned essays accompanied by previously unpublished documentation, deepening our understanding of this overlooked chapter in the history of art and technology.

Image: François Willème (French, 1830–1905). Unfinished photosculpture bust, ca. 1860. Oak and twine on base. Gift of Eastman Kodak Company, ex-collection Gabriel Cromer, 1985.0517.0001. Courtesy of the George Eastman Museum

event.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
event.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day. The exhibition includes microscope images revealing the textile structure of the woven text as well as a woven enlargement that illustrates its basic principles, along with several artworks inspired by or related to the themes of the exhibition.

event.title: The Frontier Between Legendary Monsters and Verified Natural History
event.location_name: Sapp Center for Science Teaching and Learning
event.description:
Have you ever looked at a mysterious lake shadow and thought, "Is that a giant prehistoric plesiosaur, or just an extraordinarily dramatic floating log?"

If so, step into the corridors of the Science Library for our featured book display exploring where ancient myth meets rigorous evolutionary biology. We’re separating biological facts from blurry photographs, blurry folklore, and very clear hoaxes.

Come for the ancient folklore, stay for the cold, hard science—and remember: the truth is in here, but so are the quiet study hours.

event.description:
Enjoy the gift of time in nature as a catalyst for the Contemplation by Design experience of PEACE: Pausing, Exhaling, Attending, Connecting and Expressing. Delight in connecting with nature and enhancing your connection with yourself and with others. Observe first-hand what Stanford researchers, including Gretchen Daily and Abby King, reported in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Science, namely that walking in nature can enhance emotional health.

Feel better while learning natural history of the Santa Cruz Mountains and research discoveries conducted on the majestic trails and animal life in Jasper Ridge Biological Preserve ('Ootchamin 'Ooyakma). Studies include ones that are part of a growing body of research exploring the connection between nature and human well-being. The Natural Capital Project, led by Daily, has been at the forefront of this work. The project focuses on quantifying the value of natural resources to the public and predicting benefits from investments in nature.

During your hike, you will be offered opportunities to contemplate and savor your experience which will be led by a Jasper Ridge docent for groups of 10 people per docent.

NOTE: To minimize impact on Jasper Ridge, CBD participants will carpool from the parking lot at the intersection of Searsville Road and Campus Drive West, near the Central Energy Facility at 140 Searsville Road. Marguerite Shuttles will carpool groups to and from Jasper Ridge. Please be in the Searsville Parking lot in the area near Fremont Road close to the Central Energy Facility ready to board the shuttle to Jasper Ridge at 9:20am for the morning group for which you will register.

Please visit the Contemplation By Design website to register for the morning hike
time slot. https://med.stanford.edu/contemplation/summit.html

There also will be an afternoon hike that meets on campus at 12:20pm. If you want to register for the afternoon hike you can do that on the Contemplation By Design website.

A tour is typically 1.5 to 2.0 hours. These hikes will be similar in the level of exertion called for when walking the Stanford DISH. Visitors to Jasper Ridge are advised to wear long pants and closed-toe walking shoes or hiking boots. Please bring a sun hat, sunscreen, and 1.5-2.0 liters of water to carry with you. If the forecast calls for rain, we recommend dressing in layers and bringing a waterproof jacket or poncho. Food is not allowed on Jasper Ridge trails. Please note that pets, including service/support animals, and children under 14 are not allowed on Jasper Ridge trails. (More details for Jasper Ridge information is available at http://jrbp.stanford.edu/tours.php).

Jasper Ridge is about a 20-minute car ride from the main Stanford University campus. Thus, expect to return to your car on campus approximately 3 hours after your start meeting time. The afternoon group meets on campus at 9:20am will return to the parking lot at approximately 12:20pm.

This session is part of the FREE Contemplation by Design Summit, Oct. 14-25, 2026.

The full summit schedule is posted at: https://med.stanford.edu/contemplation/summit.html

event.title: Volunteering at Stanford Educational Farm
event.description:
Volunteers help keep the farm running. Volunteer tasks vary from week to week. Farm tasks may include keeping our fields free of weeds and rocks, planting new crop rotations, deadheading flowers, teaming up on irrigation, composting, mulching, and having a great time getting dirty. We ask that volunteers come prepared with close-toed shoes and clothes you don't mind getting dirty! We have gloves and tools for all.

We welcome volunteers 10 years old and older. Those between 10 and 14 years old are required to have a guardian actively volunteering alongside them for the duration of the volunteer session.

We reserve the right to cancel volunteer sessions up to two hours in advance. Possible reasons for cancelation are a change in COVID-19 guidelines as outlined by the University or County Officials, excessive heat (90 degree and above), poor air quality, rain or other inclement weather.

We encourage all volunteers to carpool, bike, ride public transportation; there is a charge for parking on all Stanford property. The farm is not responsible for any tickets incurred while volunteering.

event.title: A Vision of Paris: The Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford
event.description:
Stanford University Libraries presents A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford, on view in the Peterson Gallery and Munger Rotunda of the Cecil H. Green Library from September 22, 2026 to January 24, 2027. 

Roxane Debuisson (1927–2018) dedicated sixty years to documenting the transformation of the city of Paris during the nineteenth century.  If Roxane Debuisson could not stop the changes she saw underway in the late 20th century, she could at least preserve the city’s earlier history through images, literature, guidebooks, and other documents. 

Her lifelong project helped to document Paris during the nineteenth century, especially the city’s rapid changes from the 1850s to the 1870s, when Emperor Napoleon III and his prefect of the Seine, Baron Eugène Haussmann, transformed the city with new boulevards, green spaces, and public utilities, and fostered innovations in commercial and cultural practices. 

A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford draws upon the extensive array of commercial almanacs, prints, postcards, commercial ephemera, stereographs, manuscripts, historic photographs, and other items that are a part of the Roxane Debuisson Collection of Paris history, circa 1789-1970, acquired by the Department of Special Collections at Stanford University Libraries in 2020. These materials place Paris as the birthplace of political, commercial, and urban innovations, and as a city defined by the tension between its historical past and its continuous reinvention. The exhibit highlights the city’s rapid changes and their diverse causes, while suggesting the collection’s vast possibilities for both research and instruction.

This exhibition is curated by Sarah Sussman, Assistant University Librarian for Collections and Services & Curator of French and Italian Collections, Stanford University Libraries, and Chloe Summers Edmondson, Assistant Professor of French at the University of Miami. Produced and designed by Deardra Fuzzell, with assistance from Kylee Jo Diedrich, Sofia McGullam Ornelas, and Pasha Tope.

A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford will be open to the public. Registration at the entrance with a valid government ID is required to enter the Cecil H. Green Library and view the exhibit.

event.title: In Focus: Asian American Art from the Collection
event.description:
In Focus: Asian American Art from the Collection showcases recent acquisitions made through the Cantor’s Asian American Art Initiative (AAAI), offering a glimpse into one of the fastest-growing areas of the museum’s collection. Many of the works on view are being presented for the first time.

Founded in 2018 by Stanford art history professor Marci Kwon and Cantor associate curator of modern and contemporary art Aleesa Pitchamarn Alexander, the AAAI is one of the nation's leading museum initiatives dedicated to Asian American art. What began with approximately 30 works by Asian American artists has grown to more than 800 through acquisitions, exhibitions, publications, archival research, and community collaboration.

Rather than presenting a single definition of Asian American art, In Focus highlights its remarkable breadth. Spanning generations, media, and artistic approaches, the exhibition brings together works by artists of Asian descent working in the United States whose practices reflect a wide range of histories, perspectives, and creative concerns. Featuring works by Pacita Abad, Ching Ho Cheng, Tseng Kwong Chi, Young Joon Kwak, Masami Teraoka, and Rupy C. Tut, among others.

IMAGE: Pacita Abad (American, born in the Philippines, 1946–2004), If My Friends Could See Me Now, 1993. Lithograph with pulp-painted chine-collé and metallic powder on handmade paper. Cantor Arts Center, Stanford University. Robert E. and Mary B. P. Gross Fund, 2023.113. © Pacita Abad Art Estate LLC

event.title: CBD 2026: Afternoon Jasper Ridge Biological Preserve ‘Ootchamin ‘Ooyakma, Contemplative Hikes in Nature
event.directions: Meet at 140 Searsville Road. Park inside the Searsville Parking Lot. Registered people will board a shuttle to JRBP in the area inside the Searsville Parking Lot that is nearest to the corner of Fremont Road and Searsville Road.
keywords: alleviation of individual and collective suffering
event.description:
Enjoy the gift of time in nature as a catalyst for the Contemplation by Design experience of PEACE: Pausing, Exhaling, Attending, Connecting and Expressing. Delight in connecting with nature and enhancing your connection with yourself and with others. Observe first-hand what Stanford researchers, including Gretchen Daily and Abby King, reported in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Science, namely that walking in nature can enhance emotional health.

Feel better while learning natural history of the Santa Cruz Mountains and research discoveries conducted on the majestic trails and animal life in Jasper Ridge Biological Preserve ('Ootchamin 'Ooyakma). Studies include ones that are part of a growing body of research exploring the connection between nature and human well-being. The Natural Capital Project, led by Daily, has been at the forefront of this work. The project focuses on quantifying the value of natural resources to the public and predicting benefits from investments in nature.

During your hike, you will be offered opportunities to contemplate and savor your experience which will be led by a Jasper Ridge docent for groups of 10 people per docent.

NOTE: To minimize impact on Jasper Ridge, CBD participants will carpool from the parking lot at the intersection of Searsville Road and Campus Drive West, near the Central Energy Facility at 140 Searsville Road. Marguerite Shuttles will carpool groups to and from Jasper Ridge. Please be in the Searsville Parking lot in the area near Fremont Road close to the Central Energy Facility ready to board the shuttle to Jasper Ridge at 12:20pm for the afternoon group for which you will register.

Please visit the Contemplation By Design website to register for the afternoon hike time slot. https://med.stanford.edu/contemplation/summit.html

There also will be a morning hike that meets on campus at 9:20am. If you want to register for the morning hike you can do that on the Contemplation By Design website.

A tour is typically 1.5 to 2.0 hours. These hikes will be similar in the level of exertion called for when walking the Stanford DISH. Visitors to Jasper Ridge are advised to wear long pants and closed-toe walking shoes or hiking boots. Please bring a sun hat, sunscreen, and 1.5-2.0 liters of water to carry with you. If the forecast calls for rain, we recommend dressing in layers and bringing a waterproof jacket or poncho. Food is not allowed on Jasper Ridge trails. Please note that pets, including service/support animals, and children under 14 are not allowed on Jasper Ridge trails. (More details for Jasper Ridge information is available at http://jrbp.stanford.edu/tours.php).

Jasper Ridge is about a 20-minute car ride from the main Stanford University campus. Thus, expect to return to your car on campus approximately 3 hours after your start meeting time. The afternoon group meets on campus at 12:20pm will return to the parking lot at approximately 3:20pm.

This session is part of the FREE Contemplation by Design Summit, Oct. 14-25, 2026.

The full summit schedule is posted at: https://med.stanford.edu/contemplation/summit.html

event.title: Gallery Conversations | JANE!
event.description:
Join us for casual in-gallery conversations in our special exhibition, JANE!, facilitated by our Museum Engagement Guides. Enjoy a spotlight tour focusining on a single object, followed by an open conversation. 

Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

From her elegant French gowns to a colossal painting of her jewels, from the Egyptian artifacts she acquired for her fledgling museum to a container of her beauty cream excavated from her Palo Alto mansion destroyed in the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, JANE! presents various idiosyncratic artifacts of Stanford lore—many of them shown for the very first time—and very probably for the last.

We gratefully acknowledge lead support for JANE! provided by Pamela and David Hornik. Sustained support generously provided by The C. Diane Christensen Fund for African Art.

---

Public tours are free for all. Please check in at the visitor services desk* in the main museum lobby.

*If you plan to bring a large group with you (10 people or more), please notify us one week in advance via this form so we can inform our Guides. Thank you!

event.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
event.description:
Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material.

Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions. Institutional Seat (2022) modifies a standard bench from the museum’s galleries into a version that is more comfortable for all museum visitors. Surround Sound (2022) attends to the floor of the gallery with dance-floor materials. Over the course of the exhibition, this floor will collect marks made by visitors’ shoes, strollers, and wheelchair treads, like another form of tally or notation.

Carolyn Lazard (b. 1987) is a New York-based artist whose primary medium is iteration. They also work across video, sculpture, installation, and performance. Their practice remembers the generative incapacity of debility.

Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is organized by the Cantor Arts Center, presenting work originally co-commissioned by the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis; the Institute of Contemporary Art, University of Pennsylvania; and Nottingham Contemporary, and is curated by Christina Linden, Director of Academic and Public Programs. We gratefully acknowledge support from The Lynn Krywick Gibbons Gallery Exhibitions Fund at the Cantor Arts Center.

Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. event.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
event.description:
Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France. Though commercially unsuccessful, these experiments laid the groundwork for the scanning, machining, and printing technologies ubiquitous today. Bringing together these rare artifacts, the exhibition opens up a little-known chapter of history to reveal the roots and richness of our contemporary world. An accompanying catalogue features four newly commissioned essays accompanied by previously unpublished documentation, deepening our understanding of this overlooked chapter in the history of art and technology.

event.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
event.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day. The exhibition includes microscope images revealing the textile structure of the woven text as well as a woven enlargement that illustrates its basic principles, along with several artworks inspired by or related to the themes of the exhibition.

event.title: A Vision of Paris: The Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford
event.description:
Stanford University Libraries presents A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford, on view in the Peterson Gallery and Munger Rotunda of the Cecil H. Green Library from September 22, 2026 to January 24, 2027. 

Roxane Debuisson (1927–2018) dedicated sixty years to documenting the transformation of the city of Paris during the nineteenth century.  If Roxane Debuisson could not stop the changes she saw underway in the late 20th century, she could at least preserve the city’s earlier history through images, literature, guidebooks, and other documents. 

Her lifelong project helped to document Paris during the nineteenth century, especially the city’s rapid changes from the 1850s to the 1870s, when Emperor Napoleon III and his prefect of the Seine, Baron Eugène Haussmann, transformed the city with new boulevards, green spaces, and public utilities, and fostered innovations in commercial and cultural practices. 

A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford draws upon the extensive array of commercial almanacs, prints, postcards, commercial ephemera, stereographs, manuscripts, historic photographs, and other items that are a part of the Roxane Debuisson Collection of Paris history, circa 1789-1970, acquired by the Department of Special Collections at Stanford University Libraries in 2020. These materials place Paris as the birthplace of political, commercial, and urban innovations, and as a city defined by the tension between its historical past and its continuous reinvention. The exhibit highlights the city’s rapid changes and their diverse causes, while suggesting the collection’s vast possibilities for both research and instruction.

This exhibition is curated by Sarah Sussman, Assistant University Librarian for Collections and Services & Curator of French and Italian Collections, Stanford University Libraries, and Chloe Summers Edmondson, Assistant Professor of French at the University of Miami. Produced and designed by Deardra Fuzzell, with assistance from Kylee Jo Diedrich, Sofia McGullam Ornelas, and Pasha Tope.

A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford will be open to the public. Registration at the entrance with a valid government ID is required to enter the Cecil H. Green Library and view the exhibit.

event.title: In Focus: Asian American Art from the Collection
event.description:
In Focus: Asian American Art from the Collection showcases recent acquisitions made through the Cantor’s Asian American Art Initiative (AAAI), offering a glimpse into one of the fastest-growing areas of the museum’s collection. Many of the works on view are being presented for the first time.

Founded in 2018 by Stanford art history professor Marci Kwon and Cantor associate curator of modern and contemporary art Aleesa Pitchamarn Alexander, the AAAI is one of the nation's leading museum initiatives dedicated to Asian American art. What began with approximately 30 works by Asian American artists has grown to more than 800 through acquisitions, exhibitions, publications, archival research, and community collaboration.

Rather than presenting a single definition of Asian American art, In Focus highlights its remarkable breadth. Spanning generations, media, and artistic approaches, the exhibition brings together works by artists of Asian descent working in the United States whose practices reflect a wide range of histories, perspectives, and creative concerns. Featuring works by Pacita Abad, Ching Ho Cheng, Tseng Kwong Chi, Young Joon Kwak, Masami Teraoka, and Rupy C. Tut, among others.

event.title: Electric Contrasts: the Art of the Detail
event.room_number: Bowes Art & Architecture Library, 2nd floor. Visitors: Please call 650-723-3408 for building/elevator access.
event.description:
Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail brings together photobooks and magazines to show how the revolution of photography in the late 19th and early 20th century changed the history of art. Electric Contrasts takes Kenneth Clark’s landmark 1938 book One Hundred Details from Pictures in the National Gallery as a starting point to illuminate the impact black and white photographic details of Old Master paintings had on new ways of seeing in the early 20th century. The exhibition reveals the anachronistic and provocative juxtapositions of artworks in avant-garde magazines and books which created a radically new vision that would go on to influence television and the internet.

Curated by Altair Brandon-Salmon. Bowes Art & Architecture Library hours: M-Th 9-7pm; Friday 9-5pm; Sunday 12-6pm.

Tour by Dr. Brandon-Salmon on 9/5 at 6 pm prior to Electric Contrasts Study Evening.

event.title: Gallery Conversations | JANE!
event.description:
Join us for casual in-gallery conversations in our special exhibition, JANE!, facilitated by our Museum Engagement Guides. Enjoy a spotlight tour focusining on a single object, followed by an open conversation. 

Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

From her elegant French gowns to a colossal painting of her jewels, from the Egyptian artifacts she acquired for her fledgling museum to a container of her beauty cream excavated from her Palo Alto mansion destroyed in the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, JANE! presents various idiosyncratic artifacts of Stanford lore—many of them shown for the very first time—and very probably for the last.

We gratefully acknowledge lead support for JANE! provided by Pamela and David Hornik. Sustained support generously provided by The C. Diane Christensen Fund for African Art.

---

Public tours are free for all. Please check in at the visitor services desk* in the main museum lobby.

*If you plan to bring a large group with you (10 people or more), please notify us one week in advance via this form so we can inform our Guides. Thank you!
